title: The Educated Barbarian: Hagakure analysis (part. 1)
summary: First episode of a long Hagakure literature-analysis series. NH contrasts the Hagakure's strict, authoritative code with Musashi's deliberately vague Book of Five Rings, then reads passages from the 'Idle talk in the dead of night' on clan loyalty, gratitude, responsibility and self-belief, relating them to lifting and life. He closes on Jocho's four oaths as a daily mantra.

claims.claim: He recommends reading the Hagakure yourself before his analysis so your own perspective isn't tainted by his bias; the series may last up to a year.
The Hagakure continues the Book of Five Rings theme of bushido but is its opposite in method: rigid, strict lines of conduct instead of Musashi's vague keys that leave you to find your own knowledge.
Literature analysis is one of his passions and what he studied in school.
He personally resonates with strict, authoritative codes of conduct and will read the text without sugarcoating, explaining where he disagrees.
The Hagakure is attributed to Yamamoto Tsunetomo, a retainer of the Nabeshima clan who became a monk after his lord died, having been prevented from following him in death.
He puts freedom first, so total devotion to a lord is hard for him to relate to; today almost nobody would die for their boss because they have no reason to.
Bushido blends Buddhism, Shintoism and Confucianism; it is closer to a religion than a martial code and covers every part of life, spiritual and physical, not just fighting.

The clan-exclusive attitude (only follow role models from your own group) mirrors YouTube fitness, where camps follow one program or approach and dismiss anyone outside it; this tribalism is dangerous.
It makes sense for a country to teach children its own history first so they love the place they live in; before checking if the grass is greener elsewhere, check your own.
Itadakimasu is not 'bon appetit' but closer to saying grace: thanking the food, often a once-living being, for giving its life so yours continues.
If you were born in a first-world country you should be grateful every day and feel pride, not shame, because the odds of being born somewhere so privileged are tiny.
No particular talent is needed to succeed, only the fortitude to shoulder responsibility; being dealt bad cards is not fate.
Freedom comes with responsibility: those with the most responsibility have the most freedom but take the most risk; living as a dependent costs you freedom.
Fortitude of mind always tramples the abilities of the body, natural or not.
Doubting that your curls will grow your biceps won't change the physiology, but it kills the drive you need to keep training for years.
Many young men start lifting already expecting to max out in two years; if your mind cannot picture greatness, it won't happen in real life.
The way is everywhere: you are a warrior 24/7, and everyday practice outside the gym translates into progress on the way.
Feelings run hot and cold, but you never leave the pursuit of physical and spiritual greatness because of them.
Jocho's four oaths (never fall behind in the Way, always be ready to serve, honor your parents, serve compassionately for others) repeated daily will make you unstoppable.
Never falling behind applies to pursuing, not accomplishing: ignore others' talent, speed or your age (even starting at 35); never lose in effort and greatness eventually comes.
Honoring your parents can be read broadly as honoring the life you were given, which means loving yourself enough to celebrate being here; that is where everything starts.
He started chasing strength and size to feel better about himself; once he did, he realized he could help others, which never crossed his mind when he lacked confidence.
Everything starts with a pledge: about 10 years ago he promised himself to get bigger, and his current physique started with that promise made before the action.
